article_title: Declining Enrollment in America's Public Schools: How States Can Respond Strategically
citation: Hahnel, C. & Willis, J. (2026). Declining enrollment in America's public schools: How states can respond strategically. Bellwether; WestEd. https://www.bellwether.org
title: Use dynamic hold-harmless policies or tapering mechanisms so funding adjusts gradually as enrollment shrinks, rather than permanent hold-harmless provisions
description: This principle holds that state funding formulas should phase down support gradually as enrollment declines rather than preserving past funding levels indefinitely. The brief states that hold-harmless provisions without end dates "weaken the connection between funding and current student needs, and they forestall structural adjustments". A more sustainable approach uses dynamic hold-harmless policies or tapering mechanisms, giving districts time to rightsize budgets in response to smaller student counts. States such as Colorado, Maine, Texas, and California offer temporary relief through provisions allowing use of a recent prior-year or multiyear average enrollment.
requirements: Funding formulas must be updated to account for enrollment change, and any additional investment can be drawn from savings realized from declines in total statewide enrollment
constraints: The brief notes most state funding formulas are based on historic enrollment patterns, which work reasonably well when enrollment is steady but create fiscal and planning challenges when enrollment is growing or declining
target_learners: Students in districts experiencing enrollment decline, including growing shares of English Learners and students with disabilities
target_learning_goals: Preserving adequate resources for instruction while districts adjust budgets and programming to smaller student counts
examples: Colorado, Maine, Texas, and California allow districts to use a recent prior-year or multiyear average enrollment for funding purposes as temporary relief
key_sources: Hahnel, C. & Willis, J. (2026). Declining enrollment in America's public schools: How states can respond strategically. Bellwether; WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED681594

article_title: Agentic AI and Pedagogical Best Practice: The Tension Between Automation and Learning
citation: Steve Woollaston, Brendan Flanagan, Isanka Wijerathne, and Hiroaki Ogata. (2026). Agentic AI and Pedagogical Best Practice: The Tension Between Automation and Learning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.04543
title: Implement dynamic fading: AI scaffolding must retreat as student competence increases
description: The article proposes that AI scaffolding be inherently transitional, explicitly designed to retreat as student competence increases. To prevent learned helplessness, agentic systems require robust, real-time analytics capable of distinguishing between temporary task completion and long-term mastery, allowing the AI to dynamically withdraw intermediate supports and systematically yield full cognitive autonomy back to the learner. In the matrix, feedback shifts from explicit corrections to subtle hints and eventually to zero cues as mastery increases.
requirements: Robust, real-time analytics that can distinguish temporary task completion from long-term mastery
constraints: The article notes it is hard to gauge when and how to withdraw support without hindering the learner, since generative AI provides implicit scaffolding through its adaptive, iterative nature
target_learners: students receiving AI tutoring or task support
target_learning_goals: student autonomy and independent problem-solving
examples: For essay writing the AI initially provides paragraph structures but removes the template entirely for the final paragraphs
key_sources: Steve Woollaston, Brendan Flanagan, Isanka Wijerathne, and Hiroaki Ogata. (2026). Agentic AI and Pedagogical Best Practice: The Tension Between Automation and Learning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.04543

article_title: Meta-Cognitive Insights into Cognitive Offloading: Mechanisms, Interventions, and Educational Implications
citation: Yufei Guo & Qun Ye. (2026). Meta-cognitive insights into cognitive offloading: mechanisms, interventions, and educational implications. Humanities and Social Sciences Communications. https://doi.org/10.1057/s41599-026-06621-5
title: Nelson and Narens's dynamic metacognitive model applied to cognitive offloading: object level and meta level with monitoring and control
description: The review organizes cognitive offloading within Nelson and Narens's (1990) dynamic metacognitive model, in which "the object level involves direct engagement with speciﬁc cognitive operations and task execution" while "the meta-level encompasses processes interacting with the object level, including metacognitive mon- itoring and control." Monitoring provides upward information flow (e.g., perceived difficulty), and control exerts downward influence (e.g., deciding to use a reminder). The review extends this model by distinguishing metacognitive beliefs from metacognitive experiences and by tracing offloading decisions across pre-task anchoring and in-task updating phases.
requirements: The model requires both object-level task execution and meta-level monitoring and control operating in interaction during learning tasks
constraints: The review applies the model specifically to learning contexts where internal and external strategies coexist, such as mental arithmetic versus calculators and spatial memory versus GPS
target_learners: students in educational contexts, including younger learners and learners with mathematical difficulties
target_learning_goals: strategic selection between internal and external cognitive strategies during learning tasks
examples: The review's Fig. 1 adapts the model for offloading contexts, illustrating monitoring of task performance and effort informing meta-level decisions about internal versus external strategies
key_sources: Yufei Guo & Qun Ye. (2026). Meta-cognitive insights into cognitive offloading: mechanisms, interventions, and educational implications. Humanities and Social Sciences Communications. https://doi.org/10.1057/s41599-026-06621-5

article_title: DysLexLens: A Low-Resource LLM Framework for Analysing Dyslexic Learners Insights from Online Forums
citation: Dana Rezazadegan, Atie Kia, Phongpadid Nandavong, Dominique Carlon, Jeremy Nguyen, Abhik Banerjee, James Marshall, Anthony McCosker, Yong-Bin Kang. (2026). DysLexLens: A Low-Resource LLM Framework for Analysing Dyslexic Learners' Insights from Online Forums. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27619
title: DysLexLens: evidence-traceable LLM framework with three-layer architecture and public GitHub release
description: DysLexLens is a low-resource LLM framework that transforms noisy social media posts into a dictionary-driven corpus, performs knowledge-graph-based question reasoning, generates verifiable responses, and evaluates them quantitatively and through human-grounded assessment. It is applied to dyslexia-AI Reddit data with 30 questions, and the article states that "DysLexLens, sample data, questions and evaluation results are available at Github1 to support reproducibility." Responses are generated with gpt-4o-mini and carry inline source-chunk references.
requirements: A reusable knowledge graph is constructed from the filtered corpus before query reasoning and is built once rather than dynamically reconstructed per query.
A concept dictionary aligned with the research objectives is needed for the filtering step.
constraints: Reddit discussions do not represent all dyslexic learners, and LLM-based triple extraction and retrieval may introduce noise; the graph should be treated as an interpretive aid rather than a complete representation of learner experience.
target_learners: Dyslexic learners and related stakeholders in online forum communities
target_learning_goals: Understanding how dyslexic learners use and perceive AI tools for learning support
examples: Applied to Reddit data collected from 50 screened subreddits, filtered from 23,480 posts and comments down to a focused dataset of 319 posts from 27 subreddits using a five-concept dictionary (dyslexia, AI, technology, learning support, perception).
key_sources: Dana Rezazadegan, Atie Kia, Phongpadid Nandavong, Dominique Carlon, Jeremy Nguyen, Abhik Banerjee, James Marshall, Anthony McCosker, Yong-Bin Kang. (2026). article_title: Dynamic Learning Solutions: A System for Personalized Educational Video Generation
citation: Siddhanth Sridhar, Shreya Chaurasia, Baddela Sai Yaswantha Reddy, Deepak Parmar, and Dr. Shylaja S S. (2026). Dynamic Learning Solutions: A System for Personalized Educational Video Generation. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14408
title: Dynamic Learning Solutions pipeline: PDF-to-video educational explanation system
description: An automated pipeline that converts uploaded PDFs into video answers to user queries. A RAG model retrieves relevant content and generates a multi-scene script with narration and "visual prompts aligned with the textbook's explanatory style"; Stable Diffusion generates scene images, DynamiCrafter animates them, Google TTS produces synchronized narration, and MoviePy assembles the final video in a Streamlit interface. The system handles both text and visual elements for multi-modal retrieval.
requirements: A user-uploaded PDF document and a user query as inputs
LLM backend (Groq llama-3.1-70b-versatile or Ollama llama3.2) with temperature 0 for consistent outputs
constraints: The RAG stage is optimized for NCERT textbook structure, so it performs better on content from those textbooks
target_learners: school students using NCERT textbooks in India
target_learning_goals: explaining textbook concepts through query-driven video explanations
examples: For each query, the system retrieved relevant textbook content, generated a multi-scene explanatory script, and produced synchronized visuals and narration

article_title: Dynamic Assessment of Young Children: Educational and Intervention Perspectives
citation: Tzuriel, D. (2000). Dynamic Assessment of Young Children: Educational and Intervention Perspectives. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1009032414088
title: Dynamic/interactive assessment grounded in Vygotsky's zone of proximal development and Feuerstein's mediated learning experience
description: Dynamic/interactive assessment (DA) is an assessment approach motivated by the inadequacy of conventional static tests, which fail "to provide accurate information about the individual's learning ability, specific deficient functions, change processes, and mediational strategies that are responsible for cognitive modifiability." The review states that "the theoretical foundations of the presented research derive from Vygotsky's sociocultural theory, specifically the zone of proximal development concept, and Feuerstein's mediated learning experience theory." DA is used with young children in educational and intervention contexts to assess learning potential rather than static performance.
requirements: An examiner mediates during assessment so that change processes and mediational strategies responsible for cognitive modifiability can be observed, rather than only static performance.
constraints: The review notes that crucial issues of cost-effectiveness, training, reliability and validity, and generalization remain to be addressed.
target_learning_goals: assessing learning potential and cognitive modifiability
learning how to learn skills

article_title: Taking Control: Stealth Assessment of Deterministic Behaviors Within a Game-Based System
citation: Erica L. Snow, Aaron D. Likens, Laura K. Allen, & Danielle S. McNamara. (2016). Taking Control: Stealth Assessment of Deterministic Behaviors Within a Game-Based System. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0085-5
title: Dynamic analyses of log data (random walks and Hurst exponents) as stealth assessment of behavioral control
description: This framework holds that log data from adaptive learning environments, combined with dynamic systems analyses, can unobtrusively classify students' behavior patterns as deterministic or random while they learn. Random walks visualize each student's trajectory across categorical choices over time, while Hurst exponents quantify persistence: "0.5 < H ≤ 1 indicates persistent (deterministic or controlled) behavior, H = 0.5 signifies random behavior, and 0 ≤ H < 0.5 denotes antipersistent behavior." The article presents this as a stealth alternative to obtrusive self-report measures, which it argues fail to capture dynamic, fine-grained behavior change.
requirements: Log data collection must be intentionally programmed into the system; it is not built into all computerized systems
Numerous data points are needed to reliably calculate Hurst exponents
constraints: The methods must be applied to temporal data
Replication of an in-depth dataset of over 11,000 interactions is difficult; the authors suggest entropy calculations as a lower-data alternative
target_learners: high school students using game-based intelligent tutoring systems
target_learning_goals: self-explanation and reading comprehension strategy use
examples: Random walks traced each of 40 students' sequences of choices among four feature categories on orthogonal vectors, yielding a unique walk per student
key_sources: Erica L. Snow, Aaron D. Likens, Laura K. Allen, & Danielle S. McNamara. (2016). Taking Control: Stealth Assessment of Deterministic Behaviors Within a Game-Based System. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0085-5

article_title: Demystifying cognitive flexibility: Implications for clinical and developmental neuroscience
citation: Dajani, D. R., & Uddin, L. Q. (2015). Demystifying cognitive flexibility: Implications for clinical and developmental neuroscience. Trends in Neurosciences. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tins.2015.07.003
title: Dynamic functional connectivity as an analytic approach for relating brain dynamics to cognitive flexibility
description: Dynamic functional connectivity is described as "a new analytic approach" that "attempts to account for variations in brain network topology as a function of time". The review presents it as a tool for quantifying time-varying functional connectivity, commonly implemented with a sliding window approach in fMRI data. It proposes this approach will enable insights into the levels of neural flexibility required for optimal cognitive flexibility in typical and atypical development.
requirements: Quantifies changes in functional connectivity metrics over time
Sliding window approach uses a fixed-length time window shifted by a fixed number of data points
constraints: The functional significance of dynamic functional connectivity in the brain is still under investigation
target_learning_goals: characterizing neural flexibility underlying cognitive flexibility

article_title: Do children with dyslexia present a handwriting deficit? Impact of word orthographic and graphic complexity on handwriting and spelling performance
citation: Gosse, C., & Van Reybroeck, M. (2020). Do children with dyslexia present a handwriting deficit? Impact of word orthographic and graphic complexity on handwriting and spelling performance. Research in Developmental Disabilities, 97(1), 14. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ridd.2019.103553
title: Educational and clinical supports for dyslexia should address the graphomotor aspects of writing, not only spelling
description: Because children with dyslexia were more disrupted by the graphic complexity of words than both matched control groups, the authors conclude that "children with dyslexia struggle with the graphomotor aspects of writing". Supports for dyslexia should therefore target handwriting and graphomotor skills in addition to spelling. The article states these findings "have potential implications for educational and clinical supports".
requirements: Supports should be informed by assessment of handwriting under varying graphic complexity, as in the tablet dictation task
constraints: The article reports potential implications; it did not itself evaluate an intervention
target_learning_goals: handwriting quality and speed alongside spelling
examples: The study manipulated graphic complexity (simple vs. difficult words) on a digital tablet to isolate graphomotor difficulty

article_title: The Case for Dynamic Models of Learners' Ontologies in Physics
citation: Ayush Gupta, David Hammer, Edward F. Redish. (2008). The Case for Dynamic Models of Learners' Ontologies in Physics. Journal of the Learning Sciences. https://www.tandfonline.com/journals/hlns20
title: Dynamic ontologies account: ontological reasoning is flexible and context-dependent
description: The authors' alternative account holds that entities may have multiple or ambiguous ontological categorizations and that a person's ontological view of an entity is sensitive to context and can vary moment to moment. They argue "that expert ontologies are dynamic and context-dependent as well", and that resources associated with one ontological category are often marshaled productively for understanding concepts in another. Ontological blending is presented as an essential expert skill for concepts like energy, flow, and quantum particles.
requirements: Models of learner knowledge must allow multiple, context-sensitive categorizations of the same concept
constraints: The account is argued from examples in everyday speech, expert discourse, and classroom reasoning rather than from controlled experiments
target_learning_goals: ontological flexibility in reasoning about physics concepts
key_sources: Ayush Gupta, David Hammer, Edward F. Redish. (2008). The Case for Dynamic Models of Learners' Ontologies in Physics. Journal of the Learning Sciences. https://www.tandfonline.com/journals/hlns20

article_title: Scientific reasoning abilities in kindergarten: dynamic assessment of the control of variables strategy
citation: Joep van der Graaf, Eliane Segers, Ludo Verhoeven. (2015). Scientific reasoning abilities in kindergarten: dynamic assessment of the control of variables strategy. Instr Sci 43:381–400. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-015-9344-y
title: Dynamic hands-on ramp task for assessing kindergartners' CVS use across four variable-count levels
description: A dynamic assessment tool adapted from Chen and Klahr's ramp task in which children design hands-on experiments with two ramps, manipulating up to four variables: "ball type (i.e. weight), steepness of the slope (i.e. incline), starting gate (i.e. distance), and surface texture (i.e. friction)". Children start with one variable to set and advance one level when at least one experiment is designed correctly, up to Level 4 with all four variables. Feedback follows each experiment, and two scores are obtained: experiment correct score (max 16) and variable correct score (max 40).
requirements: An experimenter provides guidance and feedback after each experiment, explaining correct designs and demonstrating correct variable settings when the child's design is incorrect
Variables are explicitly introduced at the start, with children interacting with them and reproducing their names
constraints: Administered individually in a single session of about 45 minutes by a trained experimenter, not in ordinary classroom settings
target_learning_goals: designing unconfounded multivariable experiments (control of variables strategy)
examples: Children designed a minimum of four experiments at Level 1 and could proceed to Level 4, where 14 of 21 children correctly designed at least one four-variable experiment

article_title: Addressing complexities in self-regulated learning: a focus on contextual factors, contingencies, and dynamic relations
citation: Ben-Eliyahu, A., & Bernacki, M. L. (2015). Addressing complexities in self-regulated learning: a focus on contextual factors, contingencies, and dynamic relations. Metacognition and Learning, 10, 1–13. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-015-9134-6
title: Dynamic relations: SRL as an iterative, cyclical process in which processes influence one another
description: The article defines dynamic relations as occurring "when two or more SRL processes influence one another". Because process models conceptualize SRL as iterative and cyclical, activity in one cycle can affect activities within that cycle and subsequent cycles. The article traces this idea from Zimmerman's feedback-loop formalization through Butler and Winne's recursive relations to refined accounts of motivational constructs as precursors, mediators, and outcomes of SRL processes.
requirements: Longitudinal data on two related constructs over three or more periods to examine dynamic relations with cross-lagged path analyses
target_learning_goals: relations among motivation, metacognition, and learning behavior
examples: Bernacki et al. (2015) examine minute-to-minute relationships between self-efficacy judgments, help seeking, and problem-solving attempts; Lichtinger and Kaplan (2015) examine relations between goals, affect, and actions

article_title: Evolutionary Perspective on Human Cognitive Architecture in Cognitive Load Theory: a Dynamic, Emerging Principle Approach
citation: Kalyuga, S. (2023). Evolutionary Perspective on Human Cognitive Architecture in Cognitive Load Theory: a Dynamic, Emerging Principle Approach. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09812-7
title: Dynamic emerging-principle view: natural information processing systems gain new principles with increasing complexity
description: The paper's first proposed modification views natural information processing systems as dynamically evolving, with new principles added at higher levels of complexity. A downward extrapolation suggests three principles (information store, randomness as genesis, environmental organizing and linking) could apply even to simple non-organic systems such as atoms, while all five apply to complex organic and biological systems. The paper concludes that "the basic information processing principles used by cognitive load theory apply in attenuated form even to non-organic systems associated with physics and chemistry".
requirements: Information is treated as an attribute of objects of any nature representing stable patterns in their organization
constraints: The paper states such specification of applicability is not critical to the theory, as the analogy's purpose was to substantiate human cognitive architecture
target_learners: human learners as intelligent natural information processing systems
target_learning_goals: understanding the evolutionary origins of human cognitive architecture
examples: Atomic shells preserving stable electron energy levels illustrate the information store principle in non-organic systems

article_title: Interventions as Probes of Cognitive Architecture: Commentary on Zhang et al. (2026)
citation: David Moreau, Kristina Wiebels. (2026). Interventions as Probes of Cognitive Architecture: Commentary on Zhang et al. (2026). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10150-7
title: Dynamic, context-sensitive view of cognition: classrooms as contexts where cognitive processes are selectively recruited
description: The article argues for viewing cognition as dynamic and context-sensitive, in which "classrooms are contexts in which cognitive processes are selectively recruited, constrained, and expressed." Ecological complexity is treated as a source of theoretical leverage rather than a confound to be controlled away. On this view, executive processes are conditionally recruited as a function of task context and representational demands, which is more consistent with the selective exercise effects than accounts treating executive function as a unitary, globally malleable capacity.
requirements: Interventions embedded within authentic educational settings, paired with theoretically aligned measurement, to reveal how cognitive systems function in practice
constraints: The article states the present findings do not adjudicate decisively between competing frameworks; they only help place constraints on theories predicting broad, content-independent modulation
target_learners: students learning within structured classroom activities
target_learning_goals: understanding how cognitive control is expressed in authentic instructional contexts
examples: Zhang et al. (2026) observed a differential pattern of effects that would likely remain invisible under more abstract or decontextualized testing conditions.

article_title: Emotions Are Not Random: Machine Learning Reveals Predictable Patterns in a 21-Day Second Language Learning Trajectory
citation: Peng Wang, Lesya Ganushchak, Camille Welie, Roel van Steensel. (2026). Emotions Are Not Random: Machine Learning Reveals Predictable Patterns in a 21-Day Second Language Learning Trajectory. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10141-8
title: Dynamic, context-sensitive account of L2 emotions: emotions as emergent episodes shaped by appraisals, contextual configurations and temporal adjacency
description: The article reconceptualizes second language emotions as "emergent and context-dependent, shaped by real-time interactions with learning activities and self-perceptions", drawing on complex dynamic systems theory and Pekrun's control–value appraisal account. It argues emotions unfold as episodes rather than stable dispositions, carry over across adjacent episodes (affective inertia), and are conditioned by configurations of contextual features such as activity type, modality combinations, pacing and spacing. The study operationalizes this account through an analytic pipeline combining unsupervised profile discovery with supervised short-horizon forecasting.
requirements: Multivariate time-series data combining momentary emotions and contextual features with preserved temporal adjacency, which the authors obtain via Ecological Momentary Assessment
constraints: The authors state profile labels are "descriptive and provisional, secondary to their utility for prediction"
target_learning_goals: momentary emotional states (anxiety, enjoyment, boredom) and self-perceived proficiency during language learning
examples: The 21-day EMA study tracked 92 learners across 6,918 episodes, identifying five emotional profiles and quantifying within-person variability and short-run dependence.
key_sources: Peng Wang, Lesya Ganushchak, Camille Welie, Roel van Steensel. (2026). Emotions Are Not Random: Machine Learning Reveals Predictable Patterns in a 21-Day Second Language Learning Trajectory. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10141-8

article_title: Developing Personalized Education: A Dynamic Framework
citation: Leonard Tetzlaff, Florian Schmiedek & Garvin Brod. (2021). Developing Personalized Education: A Dynamic Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09570-w
title: A dynamic framework of personalized education on three timescales
description: The article proposes a framework that 'conceptualizes learners as dynamic entities that change during and in interaction with the instructional process.' It classifies learner dynamics on three timescales—macroscale (months to years, developmental processes), mesoscale (days to weeks, intervention-induced changes), and microscale (minutes to hours, short-term fluctuations)—and maps each to an instructional lever: goal setting, design of instructional units/task selection, and giving or withholding assistance. It serves as a frame of reference for localizing personalization research questions.
requirements: Repeated measurements throughout the learning process to supplement and adjust the initial assessment of learning prerequisites
constraints: Decisions on the macro level are often predetermined by context and thus difficult to truly personalize
target_learners: learners across laboratory, classroom, and digital learning environments
target_learning_goals: adapting instruction to individual learners' changing characteristics
examples: The framework updates a general personalization loop (Fig. 1) with timescale-specific decision processes (Fig. 3)
key_sources: Leonard Tetzlaff, Florian Schmiedek & Garvin Brod. (2021). Developing Personalized Education: A Dynamic Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09570-w

article_title: Developing Personalized Education: A Dynamic Framework
citation: Leonard Tetzlaff, Florian Schmiedek & Garvin Brod. (2021). Developing Personalized Education: A Dynamic Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09570-w
title: Measure relevant learner characteristics repeatedly during learning and adapt instruction systematically
description: The review's central design recommendation is that personalization is most successful when 'relevant learner characteristics are measured repeatedly during the learning process' and the resulting data drive systematic instructional adaptation. Static, single-point modeling risks aptitude-treatment mismatch and can deprive learners of opportunities to acquire lacking aptitudes. Repeated measures at different timescales let the teaching agent identify whether performance is typical, whether an intervention worked, or whether a learner needs help on a specific day.
requirements: A student model that accounts for potential changes in relevant learner characteristics during the instructional process
Sufficiently dense temporal resolution of measurements to capture nonlinear dynamics
constraints: The dynamic conceptualization brings an additional load for teaching agents, who must regularly assess relevant parameters and use them for instructional decisions
target_learners: individual learners in classrooms, digital environments, and laboratories
target_learning_goals: improving learning gains through data-based adaptation of instruction
examples: ITS and formative assessment both use dynamic assessment procedures to create and update student models
key_sources: Leonard Tetzlaff, Florian Schmiedek & Garvin Brod. (2021). Developing Personalized Education: A Dynamic Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09570-w

article_title: Dynamic or Static Goal Regulation: Implications of Weak and Strong Bonds Between Autonomous/Controlled Reasons and Aims for Achievement Goal Striving
citation: Janke, S. (2024). Dynamic or Static Goal Regulation: Implications of Weak and Strong Bonds Between Autonomous/Controlled Reasons and Aims for Achievement Goal Striving. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09968-w
title: Dynamic versus static goal regulation: two accounts of how aims and autonomous/controlled reasons align
description: The article contrasts two accounts of achievement goal regulation. Dynamic goal regulation treats any aim as energizable by multiple autonomous or controlled reasons, forming goal complexes as flexible composites. Static goal regulation treats aims as agents of chronically available overarching aspirations, with intrinsic aspirations fueling mastery striving and extrinsic aspirations fueling performance striving. The synthesis concludes that "mastery aims show primarily strong bounds with autonomous reasons, whereas performance aims are more ambiguously aligned with underlying reasons", calling for integration of both perspectives rather than treating them as merely coexisting research strains.
requirements: Distinguishing aims (aspired end-states) from reasons (autonomous vs. controlled energizing forces) as separately measurable constructs
constraints: Anchored measurement of reasons after aims may artificially inflate aim-reason associations
Evidence on performance-aim bonds is ambiguous and heterogeneous across methodologies
target_learning_goals: achievement goal adoption (mastery vs. performance)
quality of motivation for goal striving
examples: The scoping review pooled goal-complex studies and life-aspiration studies to locate where bonds are strong (mastery-autonomous) versus ambiguous (performance)

article_title: Teachers’ self-efficacy in relation to individual students with a variety of social–emotional behaviors: A multilevel investigation.
citation: M. Zee, P.F. de Jong, H.M.Y. Koomen. (2016). Teachers' self-efficacy in relation to individual students with a variety of social-emotional behaviors: A multilevel investigation. Journal of Educational Psychology, 108(7), 1013-1027. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000106
title: Dyadic perspective on teacher self-efficacy
description: The article argues that teacher self-efficacy should be viewed from a dyadic perspective, meaning it is conceptualized in relation to individual students rather than only as a general classroom-level belief. The multilevel design operationalizes this by modeling students' externalizing, internalizing, and prosocial behaviors as predictors of teachers' domain-specific self-efficacy toward each student, with teachers' perceived classroom misbehavior and teaching experience as moderators. The authors state these findings "illustrate the importance of viewing TSE from a dyadic perspective."
requirements: Measuring teacher self-efficacy separately for individual students and for distinct teaching domains, as the study did with its multilevel design
constraints: Studied among third- to sixth-grade students and their teachers in regular classrooms
target_learning_goals: Teachers' self-efficacy for instructional strategies, behavior management, student engagement, and emotional support
examples: The study modeled 526 students nested under 69 teachers, predicting domain-specific self-efficacy from each student's behavior ratings.

article_title: Recent publications in history [Four articles and two books].
citation: J. C. B. (1917). Recent Publications in History. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org
title: Dynes's primary-grade program for developing the historic sense through the immediate social environment
description: Dynes's book Socializing the Child proposes beginning history in Grade I rather than relegating it to upper grades, using "play, construction work, pictures and stories" to familiarize children with their immediate social environment, including community workers and public enterprises. Grade II covers primitive life, fire, occupations and existing tribes such as Eskimos and American Indians; Grade III studies home life and customs of Holland, Germany, Japan and France, plus stories of Bible characters, Greek and Roman heroes and Columbus. The reviewer judges the work well planned and valuable for building a foundation for later systematic historical study.
requirements: Reference book lists for the teacher's use, which the author supplies
target_learning_goals: Developing the historic sense and familiarity with the social environment as a foundation for later systematic historical study
examples: Grade I familiarizes children with the policeman, fireman, mail carrier and public enterprises such as water works, parks and schools; Grade II takes up primitive man and tribes like the Eskimos and American Indians
key_sources: J. C. B. (1917). Recent Publications in History. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org

article_title: Daily affective-motivational experiences during exam preparation: Feedback loops, stability, and change over time.
citation: Berweger, B., Breitwieser, J., Kracke, B., Brod, G., & Dietrich, J. (2024). Daily Affective-Motivational Experiences During Exam Preparation: Feedback Loops, Stability, and Change Over Time. PsychArchives preprint. https://hdl.handle.net/20.500.12034/10953
title: Three-measure framework for temporal dynamics of affective-motivational experiences: carryover, instability, and variability
description: The article organizes the question of whether affective-motivational experiences remain stable or fluctuate using three complementary dynamic measures. It investigates "the extent to which affective-motivational experiences remained stable or fluctuated from one situation to the next, using carryover (autoregressive effects), instability (rMSSD), and variability (within-person SD) as dyamic measures". Carryover captures how strongly a state persists to the next occasion, rMSSD captures moment-to-moment instability, and within-person SD captures overall variability. The framework is applied to medical students' motivation and emotions during exam preparation and analyzed with DSEM in Mplus.
requirements: Intensive longitudinal (daily diary) data with repeated measures of the affective-motivational states of interest, analyzed with time series modeling (DSEM in Mplus)
constraints: Applied in this article to a 40-day exam preparation period with medical students; the article does not claim generalization beyond this setting
target_learning_goals: understanding and regulating motivational and emotional dynamics during self-regulated exam preparation
examples: The study used the three measures to show that anxiety and boredom were more stable than positive emotions and anger across the 40-day period
key_sources: Berweger, B., Breitwieser, J., Kracke, B., Brod, G., & Dietrich, J. (2024). Daily Affective-Motivational Experiences During Exam Preparation: Feedback Loops, Stability, and Change Over Time. PsychArchives preprint. https://hdl.handle.net/20.500.12034/10953

article_title: Dynamics of change in math self-efficacy, sources of self-efficacy, and math skills.
citation: Peura, P., Koponen, T., Aro, T., Viholainen, H., & Aro, M. (2026). Dynamics of change in math self-efficacy, sources of self-efficacy, and math skills. Journal of Educational Psychology, 118(2), 209-223. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0001006
title: Dynamic person-oriented account of math self-efficacy change within social cognitive theory's triadic reciprocity
description: The article applies a person-oriented, growth-mixture approach to social cognitive theory's claim that personal beliefs (self-efficacy), environmental inputs (the four sources of self-efficacy), and behavior (math skills) interact dynamically. Rather than mean-level trends, it models unobserved subgroups with differing levels, rates, and directions of change, testing what it calls the theoretical tenets of triadic reciprocity between personal, environmental, and behavioral processes. The four identified trajectories provide evidence that self-efficacy is dynamic and co-develops with skills and learning experiences.
requirements: Longitudinal data with repeated measures of self-efficacy, its sources, and skills at multiple time points
Person-oriented modeling (growth mixture modeling) to reveal subgroups masked by mean-level analyses
constraints: The design assessed sources, self-efficacy, and skills at the same time points, so causal inferences cannot be made
Only three time points, limiting the change shapes that could be modeled
target_learning_goals: Math self-efficacy and beliefs about capability in mathematics
examples: Growth mixture modeling over 11 months in grades 2–4 identified high stable, low stable, increasing, and decreasing self-efficacy trajectories related to co-occurring changes in skills and sources
key_sources: Peura, P., Koponen, T., Aro, T., Viholainen, H., & Aro, M. (2026). Dynamics of change in math self-efficacy, sources of self-efficacy, and math skills. Journal of Educational Psychology, 118(2), 209-223. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0001006

article_title: Developmental brain dynamics of numerical and arithmetic abilities
citation: Stephan E. Vogel and Bert De Smedt. (2021). Developmental brain dynamics of numerical and arithmetic abilities. npj Science of Learning (2021) 6:22. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00099-3
title: Dynamic interaction of domain-specific and domain-general brain networks in numerical and arithmetic development
description: The review's organizing framework holds that numerical and arithmetic development cannot be reduced to a single mechanism or brain region; instead, domain-specific functions (e.g., quantity and symbol representations) and domain-general functions (e.g., working memory, visual-spatial reasoning) interact on a continuum. The authors state that "The involved brain dynamics are, therefore, best described as an interaction of multiple brain regions/networks that vary along a functional continuum" (Fig. 1, Fig. 3). The framework underpins the review's account of typical development, dyscalculia, and education effects.
requirements: Interpretation requires considering task constraints, age, ability level, education and environmental factors the review lists as modulators of the networks
constraints: The review states the classification of domain-specific and domain-general is rather continuous than categorical
Many causal questions about these networks remain open because longitudinal evidence is lacking
target_learners: children from infancy through primary school
target_learning_goals: numerical and arithmetic abilities
examples: The review's Fig. 1 depicts the triple-code components (approximate, visual, verbal number representations) with auxiliary domain-general functions such as working memory and executive functions interacting with numerical and arithmetic abilities
key_sources: Stephan E. Vogel and Bert De Smedt. (2021). Developmental brain dynamics of numerical and arithmetic abilities. npj Science of Learning (2021) 6:22. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00099-3

article_title: Spatiotemporal predictions guide attention throughout the adult lifespan
citation: Nir Shalev, Sage Boettcher & Anna C. Nobre. (2024). Spatiotemporal predictions guide attention throughout the adult lifespan. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00281-3
title: Dynamic visual search task with spatiotemporally predictable targets
description: An online task in which participants search for eight upward-pointing triangle targets that fade in and out among sixteen downward-pointing distractors over roughly fourteen-second trials. Four targets per trial are "spatially and temporally predictable", appearing at fixed onsets within fixed quadrants, while four appear at unpredictable times and locations; participants are not informed of the manipulation. Data, and the experimental code (PsychoPy, hosted on Pavlovia), are available at OSF (DOI: 10.17605/OSF.IO/8UPY5).
requirements: Participants used a personal computer; the experiment did not support phones or tablets
Normal or corrected-to-normal vision and no diagnosed psychiatric or neurological condition
constraints: A well-controlled artificial environment used to maximize trial-by-trial learning of regularities, rather than realistic scenes
Cognitive issues were not controlled for in remote testing
target_learning_goals: Learning and using spatiotemporal regularities to guide attention during dynamic visual search
examples: 300 Prolific participants each completed ten practice trials and one block of 30 experimental trials with 240 targets; predictable target onsets were drawn one per time bin and assigned to distinct quadrants for each participant.
key_sources: Nir Shalev, Sage Boettcher & Anna C. Nobre. (2024). Spatiotemporal predictions guide attention throughout the adult lifespan. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00281-3

article_title: Investigating epistemic emotions experienced while reading refutation texts through a fine-grained measure of emotion
citation: Jheng, Y.-L., Catrysse, L., Van de Cruys, S., Kendeou, P., Poels, K. & Gijbels, D. (2025). Investigating epistemic emotions experienced while reading refutation texts through a fine-grained measure of emotion. npj Science of Learning 10, 30. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00324-3
title: DynamicEmo: an online sentence-by-sentence emoji measure of epistemic emotions during reading
description: DynamicEmo is a computer-based online measure developed by the authors in which participants "select an emoji to indicate their emotional experience for each sentence of the refutation text". It covers seven epistemic emotions from the Epistemically-Related Emotion Scales (surprise, curiosity, enjoyment, confusion, anxiety, frustration, boredom) plus a neutral option, allowing dynamics of emotions to be gauged across a single text and analysis at text, paragraph, and sentence levels. In this study it served as the online emotion measure during reading of eight vaccine texts, and the authors suggest it could also support real-time emotion monitoring and scaffolding in educational settings.
requirements: Participants read the full text on screen and report an emoji per sentence; single-item emoji indicators are used, which the authors justify as psychometrically sound alternatives to multi-item scales under time constraints.
constraints: The article notes different measures may capture different facets of the phenomenon; in this study the vaccine hesitancy scale was administered post-reading and excluded from analysis to avoid priming.
target_learners: adult learners (ages ~18–65, diverse educational levels, Prolific participants)
target_learning_goals: knowledge revision of vaccine misconceptions; tracking in-the-moment epistemic emotions during reading
examples: Participants read eight randomly assigned refutation/non-refutation texts about vaccine misconceptions while selecting an emoji for each sentence; emotion counts were then analyzed with Poisson GLMMs at text and paragraph levels.
key_sources: Jheng, Y.-L., Catrysse, L., Van de Cruys, S., Kendeou, P., Poels, K. & Gijbels, D. (2025). Investigating epistemic emotions experienced while reading refutation texts through a fine-grained measure of emotion. npj Science of Learning 10, 30. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00324-3

article_title: Generation and Use of Hints and Feedback in a Hilbert-Style Axiomatic Proof Tutor
citation: Josje Lodder, Bastiaan Heeren, Johan Jeuring, Wendy Neijenhuis. (2021). Generation and Use of Hints and Feedback in a Hilbert-Style Axiomatic Proof Tutor. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 31:99-133. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00222-2
title: Dynamic recalculation of the solution space for hints in open solution domains
description: For domains like axiomatic proofs where not all solutions can be calculated upfront, the article proposes generating proofs automatically and extending them dynamically. As the authors put it, "If a student takes a step outside the current solution space, LOGAX dynamically recalculates the solution space, taking the student step as a starting point." The new solution space then serves as the source for hints and feedback, so the tutor can always respond even to diverging student steps. The authors present this dynamic approach as central to their solution and suggest similar techniques would be useful for ITSs in other multi-solution domains.
requirements: An algorithm that can generate proofs and extend partial proofs from an arbitrary student step as starting point
constraints: Needed because not all possible solutions can be calculated upfront or algorithmically in such domains
target_learning_goals: constructing formal proofs
examples: When a student introduces Axiom b in the exam exercise, LOGAX builds a new DAM from the student solution and uses it to recognize and hint on solution paths absent from the initial DAM.
key_sources: Josje Lodder, Bastiaan Heeren, Johan Jeuring, Wendy Neijenhuis. (2021). Generation and Use of Hints and Feedback in a Hilbert-Style Axiomatic Proof Tutor. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 31:99-133. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00222-2

article_title: Looking Ahead to Select Tutorial Actions: A Decision-Theoretic Approach
citation: R. Charles Murray, Kurt Vanlehn, Jack Mostow. (2004). Looking Ahead to Select Tutorial Actions: A Decision-Theoretic Approach. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197308
title: Dynamic decision network for managing the changing tutorial state
description: A dynamic decision network is the computational mechanism the article proposes for tutorial action selection. It represents "the tutor's uncertain beliefs and objectives" so the tutor can adapt to and manage a changing tutorial state over time. It combines uncertain belief representation with the tutor's objectives to choose among possible tutorial actions.
requirements: Uncertain beliefs about the student and objectives must be representable in the network
target_learners: students tutored by systems using the mechanism
target_learning_goals: adaptive selection of tutorial actions
examples: Used in the article's calculus and elementary reading prototype action selection engines
key_sources: R. Charles Murray, Kurt Vanlehn, Jack Mostow. (2004). Looking Ahead to Select Tutorial Actions: A Decision-Theoretic Approach. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197308

article_title: A feedback learning and mental models perspective on strategic decision making
citation: Capelo, C., & Dias, J. F. (2009). A feedback learning and mental models perspective on strategic decision making. Educational Technology Research and Development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-009-9123-z
title: Dynamic model of decision-making process based on feedback loops and mental models
description: The article presents a dynamic model of the decision-making process in which managers make decisions and learn in the context of feedback loops. In single-loop learning, managers compare information about the state of a real system to pre-established goals and make decisions without changing their mental models. In double-loop learning, information about the business system also feeds back to modify the managers' mental models, which they then use to anticipate and evaluate the consequences of alternative strategic choices. Cognitive limitations and quality of feedback information are identified as key factors that impact the effectiveness of double-loop learning.
requirements: Managers must have access to feedback information about the state of the business system to compare against goals
constraints: Due to cognitive limitations, the mental models that managers use for decision making are necessarily imperfect, making a flawless assessment of the dynamic behavior of the business system nearly impossible
target_learners: Managers making strategic decisions in dynamically complex business contexts
target_learning_goals: Improving strategic decision making through better understanding of business system structure and behaviour
key_sources: Capelo, C., & Dias, J. F. (2009). A feedback learning and mental models perspective on strategic decision making. Educational Technology Research and Development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-009-9123-z

article_title: Using electronic technology in the dynamic testing of young primary school children: predicting school achievement
citation: Kirsten W. J. Touw, Bart Vogelaar, Merel Bakker, Wilma C. M. Resing. (2019). Using electronic technology in the dynamic testing of young primary school children: predicting school achievement. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-019-09655-6
title: Dynamic testing as a test–train–test format revealing learning potential beyond static ability
description: Dynamic testing is an assessment framework using a test-training-test format that incorporates feedback and training into the testing phases, providing information about an individual's progression in performance and cognitive functioning. Derived from Vygotsky's Zone of Proximal Development, it "focuses on the individual's potential for growth and learning abilities" rather than relying on previous learning experiences as conventional static tests do. In this study the framework was implemented computerized on a tablet, with the number of prompts needed serving as a dynamic measure of the child's need for instruction.
requirements: Multiple assessment points (pre-test, training, post-test)
Standardized graduated prompts procedure ranging from general to specific instruction
constraints: Administering multiple assessment points can be time-consuming and difficult to apply in practice
target_learners: Primary school children in the early grades
target_learning_goals: Insight into individual cognitive strengths, instructional needs and potential for learning
examples: The study operationalized dynamic testing as a tablet-delivered series completion test with two training sessions using graduated prompts between pre- and post-test
key_sources: Kirsten W. J. Touw, Bart Vogelaar, Merel Bakker, Wilma C. M. Resing. (2019). Using electronic technology in the dynamic testing of young primary school children: predicting school achievement. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-019-09655-6

article_title: Motivating factors in online language teacher education in southern Argentina
citation: Banegas, D.L., & Manzur Busleimán, G. (2014). Motivating factors in online language teacher education in southern Argentina. Computers & Education, 76, 131–142. http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2014.03.014
title: Dynamic and processual view of motivation with future selves in online teacher education
description: The study adopts Ushioda's (2009) dynamic and processual view of motivation and a holistic approach integrating possible selves and future self-guides as conceptualised in Dörnyei (2009). The authors interpret participants' initial motivation through "future selves which contain elements of who they want to be and what they ought to be", with ideal and ought-to-be selves in dialogical relationship. This framework explains why the extrinsic degree goal coexisted with genuine interest in learning.
requirements: Motivation research should contemplate mixed methods and instruments investigating both personal and interpersonal factors
constraints: Findings derive from one programme in a specific regional context
target_learning_goals: motivation to enrol and persist in online teacher education
examples: Participants' future selves included feared selves as teachers without a degree, surveyed via items on ideal identities and career prospects.
key_sources: Banegas, D.L., & Manzur Busleimán, G. (2014). Motivating factors in online language teacher education in southern Argentina. Computers & Education, 76, 131–142. http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2014.03.014

article_title: Rapid in-class assessment of handwriting using a digital tablet: Multidimensional analysis of gender and socioeconomic status
citation: Denis Pasco, Erik Gustafsson, Lucas Burget, Thibault Asselborn, Pierre Dillenbourg, Consortium Lamue, Marie Mazerolle. (2025). Rapid in-class assessment of handwriting using a digital tablet: Multidimensional analysis of gender and socioeconomic status. Computers & Education: X Reality, 232, 105311. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2025.105311
title: Dynamilis digital application for rapid in-class handwriting assessment
description: Dynamilis is a digital application that assesses the handwriting of 5–12 year old children using a consumer tablet and digital pen, scoring static, kinematic, pressure and tilt components from high-frequency pen data normalized by age and combined via PCA into a weighted total score clipped between 0 and 100. The article demonstrates its use for "rapid and in-class" assessment with 1361 second graders, capturing dynamics "not directly observable by teacher through simple observation".
requirements: Assessment requires a tablet with digital pen and roughly one minute of collected handwriting, since the app extracts reliable information from 30 s of handwriting per the cited validation work
constraints: The article notes the research context may have felt unfamiliar to some participants, potentially influencing performance
target_learners: children aged 5–12, assessed here in second grade
target_learning_goals: handwriting proficiency assessment across static, kinematic, pressure and tilt components
examples: Second graders copied sentences such as "il fait beau, il fait chaud" on an iPad with an Apple pencil while a collector observed from the back of the classroom
key_sources: Denis Pasco, Erik Gustafsson, Lucas Burget, Thibault Asselborn, Pierre Dillenbourg, Consortium Lamue, Marie Mazerolle. (2025). Rapid in-class assessment of handwriting using a digital tablet: Multidimensional analysis of gender and socioeconomic status. Computers & Education: X Reality, 232, 105311. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2025.105311

article_title: The Effect of Dynamic Assessment on Iranian EFL Learners' Reading Comprehension
citation: Mohammad Reza Amirian, Mohammad Davoudi, Mohsen Ramazanian. (2014). The Effect of Dynamic Assessment on Iranian EFL Learners' Reading Comprehension. Advances in Language and Literary Studies 5(3). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.5n.3p.191
title: Dynamic Assessment grounded in Vygotsky's Sociocultural Theory, the Zone of Proximal Development, and scaffolding
description: Dynamic Assessment (DA) is presented as a method of teaching and testing grounded in Vygotsky's Sociocultural Theory of mind, his concept of the Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD), and its related metaphor of scaffolding. Unlike traditional static assessment, which measures already existent abilities, DA evaluates learners within social interaction with a more capable other, revealing hidden aspects of ability and predicting possible future development. The study applies DA to reading comprehension instruction through whole-class demonstration in an interventionist approach.
requirements: DA requires mediation through interaction with a teacher or more competent peer during assessment
constraints: The study applies DA in an interventionist form with whole-class demonstration, with intermediate-level EFL learners aged 17 to 20
target_learners: Iranian intermediate EFL learners aged 17 to 20
target_learning_goals: English reading comprehension
examples: The experimental group received DA reading instruction over 16 sessions across 2 months, while the control group was taught the same strategies in a non-dynamic way by the same teacher.
key_sources: Mohammad Reza Amirian, Mohammad Davoudi, Mohsen Ramazanian. (2014). The Effect of Dynamic Assessment on Iranian EFL Learners' Reading Comprehension. Advances in Language and Literary Studies 5(3). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.5n.3p.191

article_title: To Wait in Tier 1 or Intervene Immediately: A Randomized Experiment Examining First Grade Response to Intervention (RTI) in Reading
citation: Al Otaiba, S., Connor, C. M., Folsom, J. S., Wanzek, J., Greulich, L., Schatschneider, C., & Wagner, R. K. (2015). To Wait in Tier 1 or Intervene Immediately: A Randomized Experiment Examining First Grade Response to Intervention (RTI) in Reading. SREE Spring 2015 Conference. https://www.sree.org
title: Dynamic RTI versus Typical RTI: two models for timing assignment to multi-tier reading intervention
description: The article contrasts two assignment models for multi-tier reading intervention. Dynamic RTI "immediately refers grade 1 students with the weakest skills to the most intensive intervention supports (Tier 2 or Tier 3)", whereas Typical RTI "starts all students in Tier 1 and after 8 weeks, decides whether students who did not respond to general instruction in Tier 1 should move to Tier 2". The experiment randomly assigned matched pairs of students within classrooms to one of the two models, holding everything else constant except the timing of supplemental intervention.
requirements: Initial screening in September using teacher reports and multiple screeners with local-norm cut points (below the 40th percentile at the school level)
Periodic progress monitoring allowing movement across tiers every 8 weeks
constraints: Studied in seven schools in a mid-size southeastern city during their first year of RTI implementation, with less than 3% Limited English Proficient students
target_learning_goals: Word reading, decoding, and reading comprehension growth in first grade
examples: Matched pairs of students within classrooms were rank-ordered on averaged screening z-scores and randomly assigned one member to Dynamic or Typical RTI; the only difference between conditions was when supplemental intervention began.
key_sources: Al Otaiba, S., Connor, C. M., Folsom, J. S., Wanzek, J., Greulich, L., Schatschneider, C., & Wagner, R. K. (2015). To Wait in Tier 1 or Intervene Immediately: A Randomized Experiment Examining First Grade Response to Intervention (RTI) in Reading. SREE Spring 2015 Conference. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED562485

article_title: Feuerstein's Mediated Learning Experience as a Vehicle for Enhancing Cognitive Functioning of Remedial School Learners in South Africa
citation: Seabi, J. (2012). Feuerstein's mediated learning experience as a vehicle for enhancing cognitive functioning of remedial school learners in South Africa. Australian Journal of Educational & Developmental Psychology, 12, 35-45. http://www.newcastle.edu.au/journal/ajedp/
title: Use dynamic assessment to obtain a more accurate and fair estimate of learners' abilities and potential than static testing provides
description: On the basis of the study's findings the author asserts that "utilization of dynamic assessment provides a more accurate and fair assessment of abilities which enables the examiner to identify the individual's potential." The rationale is that traditional intelligence tests largely assess environmentally learned abilities, underestimate learners from low socio-economic backgrounds and those with learning difficulties, and cannot suggest specific remedial strategies. Dynamic assessment instead focuses on how change can be produced within a learner in a structured learning situation.
requirements: An assessment process that builds instruction and feedback into testing, differentiated on the basis of the individual's performance
Examiners prepared to engage in active and directed teaching during assessment
constraints: The article notes dynamic assessment is infrequently used in South Africa, mostly for selection rather than remedial purposes, and school personnel typically do not yet know how to interpret DA-based recommendations
target_learners: Children from socially disadvantaged backgrounds and ethnic minorities
target_learning_goals: Identifying learning potential and cognitive modifiability rather than current attained ability
examples: The study applied a pre-test, mediation, post-test dynamic assessment sequence with remedial school learners and observed significant within-group gains after a short mediation
key_sources: Seabi, J. (2012). Feuerstein's mediated learning experience as a vehicle for enhancing cognitive functioning of remedial school learners in South Africa. Australian Journal of Educational & Developmental Psychology, 12, 35-45. http://www.newcastle.edu.au/journal/ajedp/

article_title: The Effects of Two Intervention Programs on Teaching Quality and Student Achievement
citation: S.N. Azkiyah, Simone Doolaard, Bert P. M. Creemers, M.P.C. (Greetje) Van Der Werf. (2014). The Effects of Two Intervention Programs on Teaching Quality and Student Achievement. Journal of Classroom Interaction, 49(1), 4-11. https://www.journalofclassroominteraction.org/
title: Dynamic model of educational effectiveness classroom factors as the basis for a teacher improvement program
description: The dynamic model of educational effectiveness (Creemers & Kyriakides, 2008) defines classroom factors found to be associated with student outcomes, such as orientation, structuring, modelling, application tasks, questioning, and assessment. In this study, "the classroom factors of the dynamic model were used in developing a teacher improvement program in the second intervention," delivered through a booklet, a one-day workshop, and six half-day monthly meetings. The authors frame this as an integration of Educational Effectiveness Research findings with improvement initiatives.
requirements: EER findings are used to determine the direction of improvement, requiring translation of research factors into concrete program materials and meetings
constraints: The authors state that developing improvement measures is not as easy as identifying factors that work for education and applying them, and the integration proved complex
target_learners: junior secondary students (ages 12/13 to 14/15) in Indonesian madrasahs
target_learning_goals: English reading comprehension achievement
teaching quality in English lessons
examples: The first three monthly meetings focused on orientation, structuring, teaching modelling, application tasks, questioning, and assessment; the last three focused on lesson plan development and peer teaching
key_sources: S.N. Azkiyah, Simone Doolaard, Bert P. M. Creemers, M.P.C. (Greetje) Van Der Werf. (2014). The Effects of Two Intervention Programs on Teaching Quality and Student Achievement. Journal of Classroom Interaction, 49(1), 4-11. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1100411

article_title: Teachers' Helpers: Experimental Evidence from Costa Rica on Computers for English Language Learning
citation: Sarah Humpage and Horacio Álvarez-Marinelli. (2014). Teachers’ Helpers: Experimental Evidence from Costa Rica on Computers for English Language Learning. SREE Spring 2014 Conference. https://www.sree.org/
title: DynEd and Imagine Learning computer-assisted English learning software packages
description: Two multimedia English-as-a-foreign-language software packages evaluated in Costa Rican primary schools. DynEd uses a "non-linear," blended approach presenting all material only in English (immersion), with worksheets, online teacher training, and placement and mastery tests; Imagine Learning uses a "linear" teaching approach and a "fade" approach explaining early vocabulary and concepts in Spanish, with no supplementary materials or teacher training. Project documentation reports average time spent per week of 67 minutes for DynEd and 127 minutes for Imagine Learning.
requirements: Schools in the treatment groups received a laptop and headset for every third grade student alongside the software
constraints: DynEd presents all its material only in English, while Imagine Learning introduces early concepts in the student’s native language
target_learners: Third-grade primary school students learning English as a foreign language in Costa Rica
target_learning_goals: English language proficiency in reading, writing, listening and comprehension
examples: Treatment students used computers every day for English instruction in year one and three days a week in year two, working with teachers the other two days
key_sources: Sarah Humpage and Horacio Álvarez-Marinelli. (2014). Teachers’ Helpers: Experimental Evidence from Costa Rica on Computers for English Language Learning. SREE Spring 2014 Conference. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED562994

article_title: The Effect of Geogebra on Students' Conceptual and Procedural Knowledge: The Case of Applications of Derivative
citation: Mehmet Fatih Ocal. (2017). The Effect of Geogebra on Students’ Conceptual and Procedural Knowledge: The Case of Applications of Derivative. Higher Education Studies, 7(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/hes.v7n2p67
title: Use dynamic mathematics software combining CAS and DGE properties to support conceptual understanding of calculus
description: The article recommends supporting mathematics instruction with Geogebra because it "combines the properties of both CAS and DGE in a single software package", allowing students to see algebraic, graphical and spreadsheet forms of mathematical objects simultaneously. In the study, the instructor used more than 15 Geogebra files, exploiting the dragging property to show how changes in one representation influence another. The author concludes its "effective use should be supported in the mathematics classrooms".
requirements: Instructor-prepared Geogebra files for the specific problems being taught
Same instructor, questions and activities across experimental and control conditions to isolate the software effect
constraints: The measured advantage applied to conceptual knowledge and overall scores, not procedural knowledge
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of applications of derivative (geometric meaning of derivative, max-min problems, related rates, graph interpretation)
examples: The instructor presented the geometric meaning of the derivative using the dragging property to show how instant change in x influences slope
A prepared Geogebra file for the house plan max-min problem showed the relation between kitchen area on a graph and the value of x

article_title: The Effect of Dynamic versus Static Assessment on Syntactic Development of Iranian College Preparatory EFL Learners
citation: Mohamad Reza Jafary, Noreen Nordin & Reza Mohajeri. (2012). The Effect of Dynamic versus Static Assessment on Syntactic Development of Iranian College Preparatory EFL Learners. English Language Teaching, 5(7). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n7p149
title: Use dynamic assessment as both a teaching device and a measure of grammatical knowledge
description: The article concludes that assessment and instruction can be combined: "Dynamic assessment can function as a teaching device for all that it measures, and it can test learners' reading comprehension and grammar knowledge." It recommends that teachers change their method of teaching and testing to fulfil learners' needs, and that test developers construct valid, reliable grammar tests informed by the dynamic model.
requirements: Teachers mediate items interactively rather than only scoring responses
constraints: The finding comes from one study of 60 male Iranian college-preparatory mathematics students
target_learning_goals: Grammatical/syntactic knowledge and its connection to social function, semantics and discourse pragmatics
examples: The study's experimental group learned grammar through mediated testing rather than separate rule instruction

article_title: Investigating the Effectiveness of a Dynamic Integrated Approach to Teacher Professional Development
citation: Antoniou, P., Kyriakides, L., & Creemers, B. (2011). Investigating the Effectiveness of a Dynamic Integrated Approach to Teacher Professional Development. ceps Journal, 1(1). https://cepsj.si
title: Dynamic model of educational effectiveness: eight teacher factors measured on five dimensions, grouped into five developmental stages
description: The dynamic model of educational effectiveness defines quality of teaching through eight teacher factors — "orientation, structuring, questioning, teaching-modelling, applications, management of time, teacher role in making the classroom a learning environment, and classroom assessment" — each measured on five dimensions (frequency, focus, stage, quality, differentiation). A longitudinal study grouped the resulting 42 teaching skills into five developmental stages ordered from basic direct-teaching routines to differentiation and the new teaching approach. This article uses those stage groupings as the content and sequencing basis of the DIA professional development programme.
requirements: Teachers must first be classified into a developmental stage via observation and Rasch analysis before stage-matched training can be delivered
constraints: The stage grouping was established for achievement in different subjects and for both cognitive and affective outcomes in prior EER studies cited by the article
target_learning_goals: improving teaching skills associated with student achievement gains in mathematics
examples: Teachers at Stage 1 worked on frequency of structuring, questioning, assessment and time management; Stage 4 skills include differentiation of structuring, time management, questioning and application

citation: Antoniou, P., Kyriakides, L., & Creemers, B. (2011). Investigating the Effectiveness of a Dynamic Integrated Approach to Teacher Professional Development. ceps Journal, 1(1). https://cepsj.si
title: Dynamic Integrated Approach (DIA) to teacher professional development
description: The DIA is a professional development programme whose content derives from the stage groupings of the dynamic model's teaching skills and is differentiated to each teacher's developmental stage. Its "integrated dimension" combines EER-derived teaching skills with "systematic critical reflection upon these teaching skills". Teachers attended an introductory session plus monthly stage-based sessions, developed action plans, and received school visits and feedback from the research team over one school year.

Monthly sessions allowing time to implement and revise action plans
constraints: Evaluated over one school year only, with volunteer Cypriot elementary teachers
target_learners: elementary school teachers at all five developmental stages
target_learning_goals: moving teachers to higher developmental stages of teaching skills
raising student mathematics achievement
examples: DIA teachers were assigned to four groups by developmental stage, provided with literature on their stage's teaching skills, and developed action plans revised at monthly sessions

article_title: Animation Based Learning of Electronic Devices
citation: Gero, A., Zoabi, W., & Sabag, N. (2014). Animation Based Learning of Electronic Devices. Advances in Engineering Education, 4(1), Winter 2014. https://journals.gmu.edu/aaa/issue/winter-2014
title: Dynamic media hypothesis: computer animation accompanied by explanations promotes learning better compared to traditional teaching methods.
description: The article describes the dynamic media hypothesis as the argument that, compared to static measures, animation reduces the extraneous load imposed on the learner and creates interest leading to the student's motivation to invest more effort in understanding the material. The present research findings support this argument among practical engineering students.
requirements: The hypothesis applies to computer animation accompanied by explanations, properly integrated into the teaching process.
constraints: The literature debate between static and dynamic hypotheses has not produced conclusive and consistent results clearly indicating the advantages of one approach over another.
target_learning_goals: meaningful learning of dynamic physical processes
examples: The present research findings support the argument of the dynamic media hypothesis, according to which the use of computer animation promotes learning better compared to the traditional teaching methods.

article_title: Dynamic Assessment of Incidental Vocabularies: A Case of Iranian ESP Learners
citation: Sepideh Hanifi, Mahdi Nasiri, Hesamuddin Aliasin. (2016). Dynamic Assessment of Incidental Vocabularies: A Case of Iranian ESP Learners. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 7(2). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.7n.2p.163
title: Dynamic assessment as an approach embedding intervention within assessment
description: Dynamic assessment (DA) is an alternative to static assessment grounded in Vygotsky's sociocultural theory and zone of proximal development (ZPD), and Feuerstein's structural cognitive modifiability theory and mediated learning experience (MLE). The article defines DA as an "approach to understanding individual differences and their implications for instruction that embeds intervention within the assessment procedure." DA differs from static assessment in testing goals, orientation, context, and interpretation of results, focusing on learning processes rather than end products.
requirements: Requires mediation through interaction between examiner and examinee, using leading questions and prompts
constraints: The article notes DA interprets results subjectively, considering peak performance rather than average performance
target_learning_goals: Vocabulary learning
Assessment of learning potential

article_title: The Effect of Peer-Assisted Mediation vs. Tutor-Intervention within Dynamic Assessment Framework on Writing Development of Iranian Intermediate EFL Learners
citation: Erfani, S. S., & Nikbin, S. (2015). The Effect of Peer-Assisted Mediation vs. Tutor-Intervention within Dynamic Assessment Framework on Writing Development of Iranian Intermediate EFL Learners. English Language Teaching, 8(4). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v8n4p128
title: Dynamic assessment grounded in the Zone of Proximal Development as a framework for L2 writing instruction.
description: Dynamic assessment (DA) originates in Vygotsky's Zone of Proximal Development and integrates instruction with assessment by providing mediation and feedback during the learning process. The article adopts the interactionist approach, in which "the role of another person who is a mediator and assists the learner in process of learning becomes prominent." DA "can unify instruction with assessment to provide learners with mediation in order to promote their reserved learning potential during the assessment."
requirements: Requires instruction, intervention, and feedback to promote L2 development by means of the ZPD.
constraints: The article notes that how exactly Vygotsky's ZPD triggers a change from dependent performances to independent performance via DA still needs more investigation.
target_learning_goals: L2 writing development
examples: The study operationalized DA through peer-assisted mediation and tutor-intervention conditions, both using a reciprocity rating scale focusing on bidirectional mediator-learner interaction.

article_title: Integrating Instruction, Curricula, and Assessments in the L2 Classroom
citation: Hill, K. (2015). Integrating Instruction, Curricula, and Assessments in the L2 Classroom. The Electronic Journal for English as a Second Language. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1085906
title: Dynamic assessment grounded in sociocultural theory assesses learner potential through mediated assistance
description: Dynamic assessment does not view variables as discrete and does not separate instruction from assessment. Through "ongoing collaborative engagement between an assistor and learner, dynamic assessment focuses on assessing the potential learners have for language development and their ability to overcome any problem-solving difficulties they may have with language usage". It is grounded in the Vygotskian theory of the mind, in which language learning and development are the result of inter- and intra-cognitive internalization processes.
requirements: Ongoing collaborative engagement between an assistor and learner
target_learning_goals: Language development
