article_title: Towards disentangling the polygenic contribution of dyslexia to school performance.
citation: Graell M. et al. (2026). Towards disentangling the polygenic contribution of dyslexia to school performance. Translational Psychiatry. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41398-026-04118-y
title: Partitioning dyslexia polygenic liability by relationship with educational attainment
description: The article proposes dissecting the genetic liability for dyslexia into components based on their relationship with educational attainment, using EA as a proxy for school performance that reflects both cognitive abilities and noncognitive influences. Variants are divided into those not associated with EA (DYSnoEA) and those associated with EA, the latter subdivided into concordant (consistent direction of effect in both traits) and discordant (opposite direction) subsets. This approach "allowed us to distinguish dyslexia-specific genetic effects from those shared with general cognitive and non-cognitive skills relevant to academic performance." The framework reveals that the discordant partition accounts for the highest enrichment in dyslexia genetic background despite comprising a small proportion of SNPs.
requirements: GWAS summary statistics for both dyslexia and EA to harmonize effect alleles and partition variants by EA association and direction of effect
constraints: The authors note they did not infer causality and cannot exclude reverse causation; family-based studies accounting for demographic and indirect genetic effects such as assortative mating and dynastic effects are required
target_learning_goals: understanding genetic contributions to reading and language learning difficulties and their relationship with academic performance
examples: The INSchool cohort study partitioned dyslexia variants into four subsets: not associated with EA (5,004,441 SNPs), associated with EA (1,425,359 SNPs), concordant (636,190 SNPs) and discordant (789,169 SNPs)
key_sources: Graell M. et al. (2026). Towards disentangling the polygenic contribution of dyslexia to school performance. Translational Psychiatry. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41398-026-04118-y

article_title: Comparison of dyad versus individual simulation-based training on stress, anxiety, cognitive load, and performance: a randomized controlled trial.
citation: Abbott Eduardo F., Laack Torrey A., Licatino Lauren K., Wood-Wentz Christina M., Warner Paul A., Torsher Laurence C., Newman James S., Rieck Katie M. (2021). Comparison of dyad versus individual simulation-based training on stress, anxiety, cognitive load, and performance: a randomized controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-021-02786-6
title: Use dyad simulation training to double learner throughput without observed performance cost for novice learners on complex non-procedural tasks
description: The article argues that if dyad training is as effective as individual training, programs can schedule learners more efficiently. It states "twice the number of learners would be able to utilize the same volume of resources", addressing climbing costs and limited resources in healthcare education while learners gain lower day-1 stress and anxiety.
requirements: Scenarios requiring interdependence between paired learners, such as acquiring, setting up, and operating a pacing device
Novice learners facing a complex, high-intensity clinical scenario
constraints: The study was not designed to investigate the learning effect and cannot conclude equivalency due to small sample size
Optimal dyad implementation for non-procedural versus procedural skills remains undetermined
target_learners: fourth-year medical students (novice learners) in health professions education
target_learning_goals: management of symptomatic bradycardia and other complex clinical decision-making skills
examples: In the pilot RCT, 41 students were randomized to dyads (n=24) or individuals (n=17) for a simulated bradycardia scenario, with individual reassessment on day 4 showing largely equivalent performance

article_title: Progression and individual differences in children's series completion after dynamic testing.
citation: Touw, K. W. J., Vogelaar, B., Thissen, F., Rovers, S., & Resing, W. C. M. (2020). Progression and individual differences in children's series completion after dynamic testing. The British Journal of Educational Psychology, 90(1), 184-205. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.12272
title: Use process-oriented dynamic testing rather than static testing alone to assess children's learning potential
description: The article argues static assessment cannot "discriminating between what a child can achieve with and without help", whereas dynamic testing incorporates feedback and training into the testing phases to tap "underlying potential rather than the current unaided abilities". Dynamic tests inform teachers about what children do with feedback and could support formative assessment and individualized instruction. The authors recommend process-oriented assessment because "static testing can lead to the underestimation of children's actual cognitive level".
requirements: Assessment procedures that embed graduated feedback or training within the testing session, ideally with IRT-based gain scoring for reliable change measurement
constraints: The predictive value of dynamic tests for scholastic achievement was not tested in this study and "needs to be a focus point of future studies"; classroom implementation by teachers remains to be studied
target_learners: primary-school children, especially those at risk of school failure or needing intensive intervention
target_learning_goals: cognitive potential for learning; inductive reasoning development
examples: The tablet-based series-completion dynamic test generated gain-score and strategy-process information reported by educational or school psychologists
